text: One drill hole drained an entire lake in a single morning.
November 20th, 1980, Lake Peñor, Louisiana,
a calm freshwater lake, 10 feet deep,
a fisherman out in his little boat.
On the water, an oil rig was drilling for Texaco.
Right underneath the lake, 55 miners were digging salt.
Then the drill got stuck, 1200 feet down.
Two and a half hours later, the rig started to tilt.
The drill had punched through the roof of the mine,
and the lake poured in.
A whirlpool opened up.
It swallowed the rig, a tugboat, 11 barges, 65 acres of land.
The canal even flowed backwards, making 164-foot waterfall.
Luckily, every person got out.
Unluckily, the lake did not.
Think of a bathtub.
Pull the plug, and everything goes down the drain.
The lake was the tub, the mine was the drain, and the drill pulled the plug.
Worse, fresh water dissolved salt, so the hole kept getting wider.
The official report blamed nobody.
Nobody could say if the drill was in the wrong place, or the map was.
The settlement, three years later, $32 million.
Days later, nine of the 11 barges floated back up, like nothing happened.
The lake is still there. It's just 20 times deeper.
